analysis.title: Asia What You Need to Know | The San Francisco Declaration Matters More Than the Headline Suggests (16 Nov 2026)
key_insights: The San Francisco Declaration could move restrictions on China's access to advanced AI compute from a unilateral US policy to a multilateral one. The note argues greater technology bifurcation may strengthen the investment case for the Chinese hardware supply chain.

The existing chip-control regime leaks. SemiAnalysis and Epoch AI estimates point to substantial volumes of restricted compute still reaching China, and DOJ cases give a documented lower bound on diversion.

San Francisco does not close the offshore cloud loophole but could create the multilateral framework needed to address it. Compute restrictions become harder to circumvent if allies coordinate both physical chip controls and remote access.
Scarcer frontier compute raises the value of compute efficiency. GIR says this should favor vertically integrated Chinese platforms with existing domestic compute, distribution and monetization.

Positioning in Chinese AI is differentiated. Mutual funds show relatively little interest in Chinese AI labs, short interest has risen in MiniMax and Z.AI, and Southbound has generally been buying the group except Alibaba and Kuaishou.

The author's takeaway is that the commercial question is who supplies the hardware to build a bifurcated AI ecosystem. The author would focus on China AI hardware and on where localization creates the next earnings opportunity.
